Recent experiments1 show that binding to profilin plays a crucial role in controlling the maximal polymerization speed of F-actin at cellular actin concentrations. These experiments are successfully described by a four reaction kinetic model, which predicts a Michaelis-Menten-like saturation of growth speed at high profilin-actin concentrations. In this work, we further analyze the four reaction model in terms of master equations and using the concept of two polymerization cycles, a pure actin cycle and a profilin-actin cycle and propose further experimental setups to gain access to all kinetic rates of the model. We find that varying the profilin excess leads to a profilin-dependent Michaelis constant for the growth speed. For polymerization against an external force, we identify a unique stall force as an indicator of energetically balanced profilin-driven polymerization, i.e., for the absence of coupling to other chemical processes providing energy input. We find that substitutions at this site are associated with substrate-dependent reorganization of the enzyme’s intra-subunit contact-correlation network. Together, these results provide an ensemble-based view of functional duality in Type II meso-DAPDH and suggest that distal network modulation may aid the engineering of substrate-dependent enzyme activities.

abstract: Solvatochromic dyes respond to changes in their local environment through variations in both spectral properties and fluorescence lifetime. These responses arise from the excited-state behavior of the probe, but the sensitivity of each response to a given environment can differ. In this work, we developed a multimodal phasor-based framework for two-photon spectral and fluorescence lifetime imaging analysis. To validate the framework, we imaged the solvatochromic dye ACDAN in water, glycerol, and ethanol. ACDAN showed clear spectral differences among the three solvents, whereas its fluorescence lifetime separated water from both organic solvents but not glycerol from ethanol, indicating that the two observables respond differently to the same environmental change. We then applied ACDAN to a well-described model system, the maturation of liquid-liquid phase-separated condensates of the microtubule-binding, neurodegeneration-related protein Tau into later-stage assemblies. Across Tau samples incubated for 1, 4, and 48 h, a progressive decrease in the ACDAN spectral phasor angle {theta} and increase in its phase-derived lifetime {tau}P suggested increasingly restricted dipolar relaxation in the probe environment. Differences among condensates were apparent by 4 h, whereas pronounced spatial heterogeneity within assemblies was observed at 48 h. Lastly, we evaluated the multimodal framework on Tau assemblies labeled with the fluorogenic probe Thioflavin T. As expected, this dye predominantly sensed its environment through its fluorescence lifetime, with comparatively limited spectral changes, whereas ACDAN reported microenvironmental changes in both coordinates. Together, this framework combines spectral and lifetime descriptors to characterize changes in the fluorescence response across Tau assembly maturation while retaining their spatial distribution.

abstract: The Wnt/β-catenin pathway is crucially involved in cell proliferation and differentiation. AXIN1, a key inhibitor of the pathway, scaffolds the β-catenin destruction complex in the cytoplasm, and pathway activation requires AXIN1 membrane recruitment and inhibition by DVL. Here, we discover an interplay of Wnt signaling and the cytoskeleton, mediated by direct binding of AXIN1 to microtubules via a positively charged binding site. The microtubule interaction ranges from peripherally attached AXIN1 condensates to tightly-tethered fibrillar assemblies that are inhibited by CK1-dependent phosphorylation. Moreover, a cell-permeable peptide designed to competitively block AXIN1 interaction with microtubules increases Wnt signaling and stimulates Wnt signaling-dependent differentiation of osteoblasts. In conclusion, AXIN1-mediated anchoring of the β-catenin destruction complex to microtubules suppresses Wnt signaling, suggesting a target for pharmacological modulation.

title: Reversible Interchain Associations Dominate Plateau Elasticity in Conjugated Polymers
abstract: The modulus plateau is widely regarded as a hallmark of topological entanglement in homopolymer melts and has been used to identify entanglement in semiflexible conjugated polymers. Using regiorandom poly(3-alkylthiophenes) as a model system, we show that their plateau elasticity relaxes through an Arrhenius process decoupled from segmental and terminal dynamics, reorganizes persistently under mechanical perturbation, and varies systematically with side-chain length. These behaviors are hard to reconcile with a purely topological-entanglement picture and instead support a transient network dominated by reversible interchain associations, consistent with π-π interactions between conjugated backbone segments. The results thus demonstrate that plateau elasticity alone does not uniquely identify topological entanglement in conjugated polymers. More broadly, they identify the strength and lifetime of interchain association as molecular design parameters linking backbone packing to stress relaxation, viscoelastic properties, and processability in conjugated polymers, complementing their established role in electronic structure and charge transport.

They quantify the effects of both combinatorial entropy terms and single-molecule ligand-receptor affinities. Importantly, neuraminidase is an enzyme that limits the number of host-guest bonds through receptor desialylation. Like active particles, neuraminidase activity enhances virion motility in the extracellular medium. Modeling the dynamics of Influenza A virions requires developing out-of-equilibrium multivalent models.

We find that the number of nuclei increases dramatically below $T_g$, with the effective nucleation rate exhibiting an unusual maximum at approximately $T_g-10$ K. Calorimetric experiments reveal a strong temperature-history dependence of cold crystallization of water in hydrated PMEA, which is explained by the observed nucleation behavior. We propose that the unusual enhancement of nucleation below $T_g$ provides a key mechanism linking high glass-forming ability and cold crystallization upon heating, thereby explaining the striking asymmetry in crystallization behavior between cooling and heating. Our findings suggest that a hidden nucleation-rate maximum below $T_g$ may also underlie cold crystallization in other glass-forming liquids.

title: Evaporation-induced colloidal diffusiophoresis in electrolyte solutions
abstract: Non-volatile solutes accumulate near a receding drying front, generating concentration gradients that can drive directional colloidal transport by diffusiophoresis. This dynamic spatial arrangement of colloidal particles could affect the microstructure and macroscopic properties of the dried film. Here, we combine experiments and theory to investigate polystyrene particles suspended in electrolyte solutions drying within a capillary tube. By varying the electrolyte composition and ambient relative humidity, we show that evaporation-induced ion gradients drive particles toward the liquid-gas interface and enhance interfacial accumulation, whereas slower drying at higher humidity weakens the gradient and particle migration. We use the heat balance integral method to predict the transient solute field for a receding interface and couple it to particle transport to capture the observed particle trajectories and accumulation trends. These results identify background electrolytes and drying rate as coupled controls on particle distribution and provide a predictive framework to optimize formulation and processing parameters for manufacturing slurry-based materials, such as battery electrodes and turbine coatings.

title: Conformationally frustrated epitaxy at heteromolecular interface
abstract: Precise control of molecular heteroepitaxy offers a route to multilayer architectures with well-defined interfaces. However, the role of intramolecular flexibility in epitaxial matching remains insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate the heteroepitaxy of intact 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene (BTB) on a molecular $δ$-layer composed of fully deprotonated BTB molecules on Ag(111). Combining scanning tunneling microscopy, low-energy electron microscopy and diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and density functional theory, we identify the key interactions controlling molecular packing and epitaxial growth. We show that intermolecular bonding motifs are preserved on the molecular template, but their lattice parameters and molecular conformations change as compared to a silver surface. Individual molecules exhibit distinct appearances in scanning tunneling microscopy, consistent with site-dependent conformational variations identified by theory. Our calculations reveal that the competition between molecule-substrate interactions and conformational energy produces different compromise geometries, resulting in conformational frustration at the epitaxial interface. Crucially, constraining BTB into a planar geometry changes the preferred lateral adsorption positions, demonstrating that molecular flexibility directly modifies the energetic preferences for epitaxial registry. Comparison with more rigid molecular overlayers further supports this interpretation. Our findings reveal that molecular flexibility contributes to epitaxial matching by allowing unfavorable molecule-substrate interactions to be compensated by energetically favorable conformations while preserving the intermolecular network.

title: Temporal dynamics of antigen-specific T cell expansion in primary SARS-CoV-2 infection
abstract:
Quantifying T cell response during primary infection in humans is crucial for understanding adaptive immunity. Leveraging a controlled human challenge to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, we characterized antigen-specific T cell responses within and across individuals. Notably, individual clones reached similar maximum frequencies despite differences in the timing of their peak expansion. Mathematical modeling within a coarse-grained framework suggested that variability in precursor frequency between different T cell clones could be one mechanism to explain this relationship. title: FACT frees Ubp10 from nucleosome sequestration after rapid H2B deubiquitination
abstract: Chromatin-modifying enzymes must engage their substrate, act on it and release it, but which step limits their turnover is unclear. Using three-color single-molecule fluorescence, we directly visualized the yeast deubiquitinase Ubp10 removing ubiquitin from H2B on individual nucleosomes. Ubp10 cleaved the mark within seconds of binding, without detectable DNA unwrapping, yet it did not let go: ~80% of nucleosomes remained bound after 45 minutes, and unmodified nucleosomes formed similarly long-lived complexes. Ubp10 turnover is therefore limited by release rather than catalysis. The histone chaperone FACT relieved this bottleneck by accelerating Ubp10-nucleosome dissociation. In living yeast, nuclear depletion of the FACT subunit Spt16 increased the slowly diffusing, chromatin-bound fraction of nucleoplasmic Ubp10. These findings identify FACT-dependent release as a likely mechanism for recycling Ubp10 on chromatin. More broadly, a nucleosome can sequester the enzyme acting on it, making enzyme release a step at which chromatin modification can be controlled.

title: Engineering Nanobody Conformational Switches
abstract: Conformational signaling is widely used in biology, but remains difficult to engineer into proteins. Here, we explore ligand-induced folding of nanobodies as a general strategy to generate conformational receptors for a broad range of target ligands. More specifically, we have generated partially unfolded nanobody variants that fold exclusively upon binding to their target ligand. To do so, we have introduced destabilizing mutations in the framework region, carefully tuning their stability while preserving molecular recognition. Given the high conservation of the framework across different nanobodies, this approach is broadly applicable to many other target ligands, which has enabled us to engineer conformational switches for three different important biomarkers and drugs: the pregnancy hormone chorionic gonadotropin, the cytokine tumor necrosis factor alpha, and the chemotherapy and immunosuppressant drug methotrexate. Another useful property of conformational signaling is that it can directly gate signal transduction, which we have leveraged to build an optical sensor for the quantitative detection of the pregnancy hormone in urine. Finally, conformational signaling introduces new mechanisms for the allosteric modulation of binding, which we have explored to control the affinity and dynamic range of the sensor. Our work thus establishes a rational strategy for engineering conformational signaling receptors with customizable properties and generalizable for many different target ligands.

title: IDR acquisition from human ortholog reprograms Snf11 to form HDAC-compartmentalizing condensates and drives yeast flocculation
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) regulates protein function by organizing proteins into dynamic condensates, yet how divergence in LLPS among orthologs gives rise to species-specific functional outputs remains poorly understood. Here, we show that intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) act as transferable modules whose sequence composition encodes phase separation capacity and functional outputs. Incorporating the QPGY domain from human SS18 into its yeast ortholog Snf11 yields a chimeric protein (Snf11-QPGY) that forms dynamic intracellular condensates. These condensates activate the adhesion genes FLO1 and FLO11, triggering calcium-dependent flocculation absent in wild-type cells. Mechanistically, Snf11-QPGY sequesters histone deacetylase subunit Rpd3 within condensates, reducing its occupancy at FLO promoters and promoting histone acetylation and transcriptional activation. Substituting QPGY with a heterologous LLPS-competent IDR restores condensate formation but does not recapitulate QPGY-driven transcriptional-phenotypic outputs. These findings reveal how evolutionary diversification of IDR sequences drives functional divergence among orthologs and offer a framework for engineering IDR-dependent regulatory modules.

title: E2F1 induces a G0-G1 reentry transcriptional program without changing chromatin accessibility.
abstract: Quiescent cells repress cell-cycle genes via chromatin-based mechanisms to maintain a non-dividing state, yet remain poised to reenter the cell cycle upon stimulation. E2F1, a canonical activator of cell-cycle genes, is sufficient to induce cell-cycle reentry from quiescence, but how it overcomes chromatin-mediated repression remains unclear. Here, we show that inducible E2F1 expression triggers exit from quiescence without changes in chromatin accessibility by harnessing regulatory elements with limited accessibility. Time-resolved transcriptomic analysis demonstrates that E2F1 induces an accelerated transcriptional program compared to serum stimulation. Unlike serum, which triggers broad chromatin remodeling, E2F1 activates genes within a chromatin context with limited accessibility. ChIP-seq analyses reveal that E2F1 binds target sites in quiescent cells to activate canonical cell-cycle genes. Biochemical reconstitution demonstrates that E2F1 binds nucleosomes and accesses DNA wrapped by histones. These findings suggest that E2F1 accesses nucleosome-associated DNA and initiates transcription without major chromatin reorganization. Our work redefines the relationship between transcription factor and chromatin dynamics during fate transitions and establishes E2F1 as a potent regulator capable of inducing cell-cycle reentry without changing chromatin accessibility.

title: Dual-reporter assay for selective small molecule inhibition of expanded toxic huntingtin
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expansion of CAG repeats in exon 1 of the human huntingtin gene (HTT). The resultant pathogenic allele (mHTT) produces a mutant huntingtin protein (mHtt) containing an expanded polyglutamine tract. Because mHtt drives neurodegeneration while wildtype huntingtin (Htt) remains critical for regulation of gene transcription and cell survival, an ideal therapeutic would specifically downregulate mHtt expression while preserving Htt. Small molecules are attractive candidates for HD given their ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier and amenability to oral dosing, but there remains no high-throughput platform that reports both efficacy and allele selectivity. Here, we present a bacterial assay in which exon 1 of HTT and mHTT, each fused to spectrally distinct fluorescent proteins, are co-expressed in the same cell, allowing simultaneous quantification of their expression in the presence of small molecules. This high-throughput assay isolates the effect of small molecules on huntingtin expression without confounding factors present in mammalian cells, such as endogenous Htt or human RNA-binding proteins. To validate this assay, we evaluated two previously reported CAG repeat binding compounds and used circular dichroism spectroscopy and cell-free protein synthesis to investigate their underlying mechanisms. Furamidine exhibited reproducible, sequence-dependent effects, altering the structural stability of HTT RNA and selectively decreasing the wildtype Htt expression (a selectivity profile opposite to what is therapeutically required). In contrast, myricetin did not affect HTT RNA stability and its decreased signal in the dual-expression assay was due to fluorophore artifacts. This highlights the importance of complementary workflows in distinguishing genuine modulators from reporter-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings establish the dual-expression assay as a screening platform for CAG repeat-targeting small molecules and demonstrate the importance of determining which allele reported compounds preferentially affect.

title: Nanomechanical phenotyping uncovers a non-canonical smooth muscle-like hypercontractility program in lung squamous cell carcinoma myofibroblasts
abstract: Myofibroblast-like cancer-associated fibroblasts (myCAFs) drive the stiff, tumor-promoting microenvironment, yet their mechanical phenotype in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains undefined. myCAFs from major NSCLC subtypes (lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC)) were examined combining atomic force microscopy and traction force microscopy with molecular and signaling analyses. LUAD-myCAFs displayed canonical myofibroblast features, including elevated stiffness, traction forces, ROCK-MYPT1 signaling, and -SMA-rich stress fibers. Unexpectedly, LUSC-myCAFs amplified these nanomechanical features despite reduced ROCK-MYPT1 signaling and comparable -SMA levels. Instead, they exhibited a smooth muscle cell (SMC)-like contractile program characterized by enhanced SM-MHC(MYH11) expression colocalized with -SMA, ERK1/2-RLC hyperactivation, and DNA methylation reprogramming including SMC-contractility regulators. LUSC-myCAF hypercontractility was linked with reduced proliferative capacity and smaller intratumoral vessel lumens, consistent with the low CAF density and enhanced hypoxia patterns reported in LUSC. SMC markers were enriched and associated with adverse outcomes selectively in LUSC, highlighting the relevance of SMC-like myCAFs in LUSC progression. These findings unveil subtype-specific myCAF programs in NSCLC, and identify -SMA/SM-MHC(MYH11) myCAFs as key determinants of tumor mechanics, providing a rationale for the survival benefits of antihypertensive drugs targeting SMC hypercontractility. Moreover, they demonstrate that nanomechanical phenotyping can uncover translationally relevant myCAF phenotypes invisible to molecular profiling.

title: Frequency-Dependent Structural Responses of Amyloid-β Fibrils to Terahertz Pulses: A Nonequilibrium Molecular Dynamics Study
abstract: The abnormal aggregation of amyloid proteins into fibrils is closely associated with several neurodegenerative diseases, highlighting the importance of developing effective strategies to modulate fibril structural stability. Here, we employed nonequilibrium molecular dynamics(NEMD) simulations to examine the effects of intense terahertz-to-mid-infrared pulses on three amyloid fibrils (2LMP, 2MXU, and 5OQV), focusing on the combined effects of pulse frequency and electric-field strength. Frequency scans from 0.5 to 60 THz in 0.5 THz steps revealed frequency-dependent losses of {beta}-sheet content, with several common response patterns in these fibrils. Comparisons at 2, 23, 33, and 50 THz showed that pulse-induced changes in secondary structure differed from those in high-temperature controls. Hydrogen-bond analysis showed that total hydrogen-bond counts could partially recover even as interchain hydrogen bonds continued to decrease, with distinct responses among representative chain pairs. We therefore propose a two-threshold electric-field framework for fibril disruption: Eth1 describes the onset of structural perturbation, whereas Eth2 indicates persistent structural loss after the pulse. This framework offers a testable approach for characterizing amyloid structural responses to external fields, although the underlying energy-coupling mechanisms, quantitative thresholds, and long-term recovery require further validation. These findings may provide a theoretical basis for exploring external-field-based strategies to modulate protein aggregation.

abstract: Targeted lipid nanoparticles (tLNPs) hold promise for improving cell- and tissue-selective delivery of therapeutic payloads but introduce analytical challenges associated with characterizing both encapsulated cargo and surface-associated targeting ligands within the same formulation. Conventional nucleic acid and protein assays can be affected by nanoparticle scattering, matrix interference, or a limited ability to distinguish conjugated antibody from free antibody. Here, we report an online deformulating size-exclusion high-performance liquid chromatography (SE-HPLC) method that enables simultaneous quantification of total RNA, conjugated antibody, and free antibody from 5 L of tLNP sample. Following injection, exposure to a mobile phase containing sodium dodecyl sulfate and isopropanol disrupts the nanoparticles, enabling chromatographic separation of RNA, conjugated antibody, and free (unconjugated) antibody while minimizing sample handling prior to analysis. RNA was quantified by UV260 detection, whereas antibody was quantified by UV280 or intrinsic fluorescence detection to maximize sensitivity. The method demonstrated linear response over the evaluated concentration ranges, spike recoveries of 88-122%, and precision below 5% relative standard deviation. Application to purified tLNP formulations demonstrated simultaneous assessment of total RNA and conjugated antibody content, while confirming the absence of detectable free antibody following purification. Together, these results establish online deformulating SE-HPLC as a practical multi-attribute analytical method for characterization of tLNPs, enabling concurrent assessment of total RNA concentration, conjugated antibody concentration, and free antibody concentration using standard HPLC instrumentation.

abstract: If a liquid is cooled rapidly, it may fall out of equilibrium before it can crystallize. It may, however, crystallize later from the nonequilibrium glassy state. Using the Random First-Order Transition (RFOT) theory of glasses, we discuss a variety of mechanisms of crystallization as a route to devitrification. Ordinary nucleation is sped up by the frozen in energy of the glass relative to the liquid. At sufficiently low temperatures, a mechanism of nanonucleation appears, producing nanometer scale crystal inclusions in the glass. Nanocrystallization depends strongly on the local fluctuations in stability, and the transition from classical nucleation and growth to nanocrystallization occurs dominantly through rare, less stable glassy regions that percolate through space, producing an additional dramatic speedup in the crystal nucleation and growth rates. Similar fluctuations in local stability also explain anomalies of crystal growth in deeply supercooled systems.

We develop a reduced three-sphere collision description in which trapping is governed by impact geometry and friction, while fracture inside the trapping regime is evaluated from DEM output using stress-based and contact-force-based normalized criteria. abstract: We study first-order condensation in finite open wedges using classical density functional theory (DFT) and compare the resulting microscopic phase behaviour with recent macroscopic predictions. Two geometries are considered: a symmetric wedge formed by two identical inclined walls and an asymmetric wedge formed by a vertical and an inclined wall. The DFT calculations confirm the two condensed morphologies predicted for the symmetric wedge and the three morphologies predicted for the asymmetric wedge and their emergence depending on the wedge size, opening angle, and wall contact angle. Under partial-wetting conditions, the microscopic phase boundaries are in nearly perfect quantitative agreement with the macroscopic predictions, including reentrant changes between pinned and depinned meniscus configurations and the appearance of the semi-double-pinned state in the asymmetric wedge. This shift is attributed to adsorbed liquid films, which reduce the effective width available to the gas and thereby increase the effective aspect ratio of the confinement.

title: Closed-form solution for semi-symmetric folding of waterbomb tessellations
abstract: Rigid-origami folding has versatile applications in the fields of architecture, engineering, medicine and aerospace. Given the design parameters of a single waterbomb cell, the global geometry of the origami tessellated shell at an intermediate state of folding is directly determined. Even though existing numerical methods of rigid-origami can be used to describe geometric forms, algebraic solutions of the waterbomb folding kinematics and tessellations reduce the algorithmic complexity and determine the range of admissible configurations exactly. The existing analytical solution for a symmetrically folded waterbomb cell and tessellation is extended to the case of a cell folded semi-symmetrically, i.e. a cell with a 180° rotation symmetry. The algebraic derivation provides the solution for the entire folding process. The resulting functional relationship between the design parameters and the 3D cell geometry of the folded waterbomb cell enables efficient studies of achievable shell geometries. This development facilitates a deeper understanding of the correspondence between the geometric parameters of a single waterbomb cell and the statically relevant geometric properties, i.e. the shell curvature and the effective cross-sectional height. The systematic description of this correspondence provides the basis for innovative design concepts using modern cementitious composites, e.g. textile-reinforced concrete, to produce thin-walled, high-performance, lightweight shells.

abstract: Talin is a central mechanosensitive adaptor that links integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and converts mechanical force into biochemical signals. Vertebrates express two highly homologous talin isoforms, talin-1 and talin-2, yet the molecular basis for their nonredundant functions remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how isoform-specific sequence differences alter the mechanical response and ligand-binding capabilities of the talin rod. Using single-molecule force spectroscopy and biochemical binding assays, we show that talin-2 preserves the overall mechanical architecture of talin-1 but exhibits distinct mechanical responses in key rod regions. Talin-2 R7-R9 exhibits a previously unobserved three-domain cooperative unfolding pathway, while an alternative sequential pathway reveals early unfolding of R9 at substantially lower force than in talin-1. Strikingly, talin-2 R4-R6 has acquired two additional mechanically regulated interactions: a previously unrecognized vinculin-binding site in R5 and an A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP) region within R5-R6 that recruits protein kinase A (PKA). Together with the conserved R9 AKAP site, this establishes two spatially separated, mechanically regulated PKA-anchoring regions within the talin-2 scaffold. These findings establish that isoform-specific sequence divergence not only reshapes the mechanical response of the talin scaffold but also expands its repertoire of force-regulated interactions, providing a mechanism for the assembly of different structural and signaling complexes in an isoform-dependent manner.

abstract: During kiss-and-run exocytosis, a transient fusion pore opens, releases part of the vesicular quantum, and closes without full fusion. This report investigates two questions: first, whether dense-core vesicles undergoing kiss-and-run contain the same number of molecules as those undergoing full fusion; second, whether subquantal release results from pore closure or vesicle depletion. We analyzed amperometric recordings of extrasynaptic serotonin release from dense-core vesicles in cultured leech Retzius neurons. Full-fusion events released 91,585{+/-}34,428 molecules (n=14), whereas kiss-and-run events released 58,344{+/-}20,759 molecules, 64% of the quantum. We analyzed the biexponential dynamics of the filtered amperometric current using Ohmic equations for cylindrical and toroidal pores. Hydrated flux packing (HFP) independently estimated the minimum peak pore diameter from the number of hydrated serotonin molecules crossing the pore. Kiss-and-run peak diameters were 2.1 to 3.2 nm, corresponding to the passage of 4 to 10 hydrated molecules. The vesicular serotonin content of individual kiss-and-run events was estimated by a frozen pore extrapolation (FPE), in which pores were kept at the peak HFP diameter. FPE yielded 102,650{+/-}10,989 molecules per vesicle (n=15), similar to the quantum obtained by integrating full-fusion events. Therefore, kiss-and-run subquantal release did not reflect a smaller quantum. We then compared the decay of serotonin flux with that estimated through the frozen pore at its peak diameter. In every event, the flux decayed faster, reaching half its peak in 0.59 (0.23 to 0.95) of the time taken by the frozen pore flux. We conclude that subquantal release during kiss-and-run exocytosis is governed by fusion-pore closure rather than vesicle depletion.

abstract: Abstract Mutations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene are among the most frequent alterations in human cancers, but whether quantum mechanical effects such as DNA entanglement, influence mutation patterns remain unexplored. Here, we applied a coupled quantum harmonic oscillator model to compute von Neumann Entropy (VNE), a proxy for quantum entanglement, across the TP53 sequence. We found that known mutational hot spots exhibited significantly elevated VNE compared to non-hot spot regions, suggesting that local quantum coupling may reflect structural instability or altered repair accessibility. CpG sites, traditionally linked to methylation-driven mutability, did not exhibit elevated VNE, indicating that quantum properties captured by our closed model are distinct from classical biochemical mechanisms. While these computational results raise the possibility that quantum effects could contribute to genomic instability in TP53, we caution that the analysis is limited by the small number of validated hot spots (n=6) and lacks biological validation. our findings are exploratory and should be interpreted carefully. If confirmed in a larger, multi-gene studies with biophysical measurements, a quantum informed framework could open new avenues for predicting mutation hot spots and understanding cancer mutagenesis. We advocate for interdisciplinary efforts bridging quantum physics and oncology to explore these possibilities further.

title: siRNA/mRNA payload of lipid nanoparticles quantified using fluorescence microscopy and correlation spectroscopy
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the most promising vectors to deliver nucleic acids to mammalian cells. Advanced delivery strategies involving multiple nucleic acid species require a reliable determination of RNA payload and LNP size. Here, we use total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) to determine mRNA payload and siRNA/mRNA codelivered payload. Particularly, FCS proves to be a reliable method for payload determination, independently of fluorophore properties that can be altered during encapsulation. By varying the PEG-lipid fraction relative to the reference ONPATTRO formulation, we find that mRNA payload of enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) coding mRNA increases from [~]10 with LNP size according to a power law with an exponent 1.3. Cryogenic electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) reveals that in this case blebs occur more frequently in small LNPs. For siRNA/mRNA coencapsulation the siRNA fraction within LNPs exceeds that in the initial RNA mixture, suggesting that coencapsulation is competitive and constrained by nucleic acid diffusion. Together, our findings highlight the importance of particle size and encapsulation kinetics in controlling the loading and composition of RNA payloads in LNPs.

title: Opposing Roles of Cholesterol and Cholesterol Sulfate in Proton Transfer and Diffusion at Membrane Interfaces
abstract: Sterols are fundamental components of biological membranes that modulate membrane fluidity and organisation, yet their role in governing interfacial proton dynamics remains underexplored. Here, we elucidate how cholesterol (Ch) and cholesterol sulfate (ChS) regulate excited-state proton transfer (PT) and long-range proton diffusion (PD) using a complementary dual-approach experimental framework combined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Using a membrane-anchored photoacid in small unilamellar vesicles, we demonstrate that Ch accelerates local PT dynamics in gel-phase phosphatidylcholine membranes by inducing a fluid, liquid-ordered phase. Surprisingly, ChS inhibits local PT despite its negative headgroup. MD simulations reveal this inhibition stems from deeper probe embedding within ChS containing bilayers and the reduced basicity of sulfate relative to phosphate. Conversely, solid-state electrical measurements on supported lipid bilayers show a stark reversal for long range proton conduction (lateral PD): ChS increases lateral proton conductance by 400 fold under controlled relative humidity, whereas Ch decreases conductivity. This divergence arises mainly because ChS supplies titratable sulfate charge carriers, whereas Ch dilutes key phosphate proton mediators that promote a percolating interfacial hydrogen bonding network without providing charge carriers. Our findings demonstrate that sterols exert scale-dependent control over membrane PT/PD, revealing how headgroup chemistry, membrane fluidity, and hydration synergistically govern bioenergetic proton dynamics.

title: Multi-scale biophysical modeling of fungal colony growth
abstract: Fungal colony growth is shaped by the fundamental physical operating principles of hyphal elongation, branching, and anastomosis, which collectively organize into macroscopic foraging networks. While sophisticated 3D models utilizing adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) on high-performance computing architectures can explicitly capture these discrete cellular mechanics, their immense computational cost prevents their integration into predictive ecosystem simulators. Here, building upon the Biological Modeling and interface eXchange (BMX) framework, we combine high-fidelity discrete hyphal mechanics with an analytically tractable, stochastic traveling-wave surrogate (sBARE) to provide multiscale simulations of fungal colonies at a fraction of the computational cost. By leveraging demographic fluctuations at the advancing front, our framework uniquely resolves macroscopic parameter degeneracies, separating the directed forward drift of leading tips from their effective diffusion to capture the macroscopic signature of negative autotropism in 3D networks. Simulations reproduce experimentally observed traveling wave profiles and confirm that interior network density under replete conditions emerges as an invariant self-regulated by fusion. Furthermore, global sensitivity analysis reveals that expansion speed and network density are governed by largely disjoint microscopic parameters. We demonstrate that because the physics of hyphal growth permit networks that are both exceptionally fast and dense, the empirical trade-off between sparse 'explorer' and dense 'exploiter' strategies observed in nature is not a strict mechanical constraint, pointing instead to metabolic limits on local growth rules. Our mathematically tractable approach bridges exascale-level cellular mechanics with macroscopic wave dynamics, enabling the integration of trait-driven advective fluxes and carrying capacities into the spatial transport and reaction network schemes of large-scale biogeochemical models.

title: Maximum Likelihood Localization Maps
abstract: Single-molecule localization microscopy commonly reconstructs images from estimated emitter coordinates. We calculate maximum-likelihood localization maps (MLLM), a non-iterative approach that evaluates positional likelihood from measured data and a supplied point-spread function. The MLLM of each detected single molecule image is added into a final upsampled image representing the overall molecular probability map, preserving the positional likelihood structure and obviating separate coordinate-based rendering. MLLM calculation is noniterative, fast, supports any calibrated point-spread function, accounts for local background variation, supports two- and three-dimensional reconstruction, and can be calculated in parallel.

title: Distributed Network Sensing as an Escape Strategy
abstract: The response of a swarm of ants or birds, living tissue of cells, or a robotic swarm, to spatial signals from the environment as a whole is a fundamental challenge for these decentralized systems. A promising alternative is embodied distributed sensing and decision-making, so that local environmental cues directly shape coordinated reconfiguration, growth, or movement without centralized control. Fluidic networks offer a physical basis for such systems, yet existing implementations are predesigned and limited in their ability to process spatial information across extended systems. Here, we investigate how fluid transport networks enable environmental sensing and adaptive response using the slime mould Physarum polycephalum. By exposing Physarum vein networks to dynamic pH environments, we show that the organism's ability to respond to aversive stimuli is governed by its spatial extent and network connectivity. Above a certain size, organisms with network morphology reliably detect and escape harmful conditions by network reconfiguration, whereas disconnected or spatially confined organisms fail to respond. In environments with competing stimuli, network morphologies enable integration of spatial information and repositioning into favorable regions. We identify local contractions as a physical mechanism that drives fluid redistribution and converts local stimulation into system-level responses. Finally, we generate different morphologies using fluidic and electrochemical control, demonstrating large-scale adaptation to complex environments. These results establish distributed fluidic networks as a framework for integrated sensing and actuation, providing design principles for autonomous soft robotic systems in dynamic environments.

title: Antidiffusive instabilities in active matter: granular experiments, theory and outlook
abstract:
Abstract
                  This article presents a perspective on the widespread occurrence of antidiffusive instabilities in systems in which free energy is supplied in a sustained manner directly to the constituent particles. Defining this distinct category allows a discussion of living matter as a special kind of non-equilibrium material. After an introduction surveying diverse manifestations of antidiffusion, including some in which momentum transfer through an ambient fluid plays a central role, we describe experiments and theory on a striking and extreme form that arises in a vibrated monolayer of macroscopic particles. This article has two aims: to bring active matter as a novel hydrodynamic arena to the attention of researchers in large-scale fluid and plasma flows, and to highlight open issues arising in our work with wider implications for a statistical thermodynamics of active matter.
                  This article is part of the theme issue ‘Anti-diffusive transport and layering: from sub-cellular to astrophysical scales’.

title: Lysenin Induced Membrane Curvature on Erythrocytes and Nanoporous Mica Free Standing Membranes
abstract: Beta porin toxins are virulence factors that oligomerize in host cell membranes, forming beta-barrel pores that permeabilize target cells, leading to osmotic imbalance, cell lysis, and immune evasion. Despite extensive research on beta-pore-forming toxins (PFTs), significant gaps remain in understanding their role as actors of large-scale supramolecular membrane remodeling. While beta-PFTs are traditionally viewed as passive cylindrical conduits, their biological efficacy is fundamentally tied to an evolved ability to structurally alter the host cell membrane. In this study, we combine erythrocytes, model membranes and a novel engineered nanopores on mica substrates. We overcome the limitation of traditional mica substrates and demonstrate that lysenin pores do not merely permeabilize the membrane; they curve it into rigid, dome-like supramolecular structures. Moreover, to gain biophysical insight beyond the standard membrane models which do not directly consider the membrane insertions, we propose a hybrid model combining the biophysical models and the architectural models of pendentive domes, where the intrinsic wedge-shaped geometry of the monomers is considered. Experimental mechanical assessment of the lysenins domes shows a non-linear mechanical of stiffness with respect the radius of curvature as predicted by our hybrid model. Collectively, our work suggests that the beta-PFTs induce membrane curvature by the assembly of wedges. Beyond their pore-forming function, this membrane-bending activity may represent an additional mechanism by which beta-PFTs interfere with host-cell membrane repair.

title: Microtubule stability modulates Schlemm’s canal cell mechanobiology and outflow facility in glaucoma
abstract: The inner wall of Schlemm’s canal (SC) is a specialized mechanosensitive endothelium in which pore formation is essential for normal conventional aqueous humor outflow and hence intraocular pressure homeostasis, yet the role of microtubule (MT) stability in this process remains poorly understood. Here, using SC cell primary cultures from normal and glaucomatous human eyes as well as mouse whole eye perfusion, we identify MTs as a key component of the mechanotransduction machinery linking the mechanical microenvironment to SC cell biomechanics and conventional outflow. We show that MT stability is modulated by substrate stiffness and diminished in glaucomatous SC cells. MT stabilization suppresses GEF-H1-dependent actomyosin contractility, reduces cellular stiffness, and promotes transcellular pore formation in both normal and glaucomatous SC cells, whereas MT destabilization elicits opposing effects. Consistent with these cellular responses, pharmacological MT stabilization enhances conventional outflow facility in ex vivo mouse eyes. Together, our findings establish MT-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking extracellular mechanical cues to SC biomechanics and transcellular pore formation and highlight MT-associated signaling as a potential therapeutic target for improving conventional outflow in glaucoma.

title: A generic residue-numbering system for microbial rhodopsins
abstract: Microbial rhodopsins are photoreceptors with a conserved seven-transmembrane core architecture that use the chromophore retinal—a vitamin A derivative—to convert light absorption into ion transport, signaling, and enzymatic activity. Since their discovery half a century ago, genome sequencing has uncovered thousands of these proteins across archaea, bacteria, eukaryotes, and viruses, revealing a diverse functional repertoire that includes ion pumps and channels, transducer activators, and enzyme/channel regulators. Although the structure of the seven-transmembrane bundle core and the retinal-binding pocket is highly conserved, the sequence identity across major classes is low. This low sequence identity, combined with the rapidly expanding number of microbial rhodopsins identified by metagenomics, makes direct comparisons across the superfamily increasingly difficult. Here, we introduce a generic residue-numbering system for microbial rhodopsins (MO numbering system), a structure-guided framework anchored to the retinal-binding pocket that enables consistent residue comparison across even the most divergent family members. Analyzing 129 structures and approximately 40,000 sequences, we demonstrate its utility by analyzing sequence–structure–function relationships across the superfamily, including previously uncharacterized members. The MO numbering system provides a common language for organizing the growing repertoire of microbial rhodopsins, integrating structural, spectroscopic, and electrophysiological data, and engineering next-generation optogenetic tools.

title: A High-Dimensional Lab-Frame Model of Markovian Dynamics in Alanine Dipeptide
abstract: We present a high-dimensional coarse-grained model of alanine dipeptide that explicitly incorporates global translation and rotation alongside internal conformational dynamics. Using atomistic molecular dynamics trajectories, we construct a 10-bead Markovian Langevin model with a 24-dimensional internal potential of mean force and a full matrix of site-specific friction coefficients. The equilibrium landscape is represented by a Gaussian mixture model, while a rotational-entropy correction accounts for the coupling between internal conformation and global molecular motion. Friction coefficients are obtained using a generalized Einstein relation based on time-correlation functions. We show that the rotational-entropy correction is essential for obtaining a physically admissible friction matrix and significantly affects the inferred dynamics. Without fitting to coarse-grained dynamical observables, the resulting model reproduces a broad range of atomistic auto- and cross-correlation functions. The result is a compact and interpretable dynamical representation of the entire peptide at the chosen CG resolution, which explicitly preserves distinctions between energetic and dissipative coupling over a wide range of motions, including those between conformational fluctuations and global translational and rotational diffusion.

title: Flexoelectric Switching of Lock-and-Key Topological Bits
abstract: Topological defects in nematic liquid crystals are high-energy sites of reduced order. We show that a point defect can be stabilized in pillbox-shaped pores. The pore shape promotes lock-and-key docking similar to that observed for colloidal particles. The defect docks in one lobe or the other, displaying bistability. Furthermore, the defect moves like a charged object in an external electric field. An in-plane field drives the defect from one lobe to the opposite lobe, where it remains once the field is removed. The velocity is linear in field strength and reverses with polarity, consistent with flexoelectric coupling. Within the pore, the nematic around the defect carries a positive bulk bound charge density, compensated by negative space charge in the rest of the fluid and on the bounding surfaces. The external field breaks the mirror symmetry of the pore and drives the defect motion. Defect displacement increases the component of the net dipole in the domain along the field. Antagonistic curvature in peanut-shaped pores repels the defect, allowing pore geometry to set distinct switching thresholds. The defects, while not topologically required, are long lived, so information can be stored in their position, allowing them to serve as topological bits. Arrays of topological bits store and rewrite binary information in defect positions, offering a route to reconfigurable, field-addressable soft materials.

title: Embodied physical learning: a trained bacterial cell wall can guide organism behavior
abstract: Physical learning studies how physical systems themselves can be trained to perform learning tasks using physical laws. For instance, disordered spring networks can be trained by local rules to route a mechanical signal from one site in the network to another. Disordered spring networks play key roles in many facets of cell biology, not just in terms of mechanics, but also in terms of motility. How then can training on the substrate itself impact the action of an organism, such as a bacterium? Here, we train a spring-network model of the bacterial cell wall and embed it in a motile agent. The stimulus is the load the cell generates by colliding with a surface. The trained wall routes that load across the body to distant flagellar motors, where it drives stator release, and the resulting turn biases the cell toward escape and delays subsequent surface contacts. On the first near-wall tumble after entrapment, the trained cell recovers 89% of the advantage an ideal side-resolved controller provides. We call this arrangement embodied physical learning: the stimulus, the actuator, and the consequences all belong to the agent, and the training force scale is inherited from the agent's own sensing rather than imposed. An actuator with its own kinetics imposes a second, tighter constraint: the routed signal must switch the actuator within the stimulus window. We also find that behavior converges within a few hundred wall encounters, comparable to what a cell in sustained contact with structure experiences in a single generation, and that the routing survives continuous crosslink remodeling provided crucial, tension-bearing bonds are protected. Experimental tests of embodied physical learning are discussed.

Here, we experimentally investigate how the partitioning of anionic PFAS affects the surface charge of phospholipid vesicles and consequently, their electrokinetically driven vesicle motion, in particular diffusiophoresis. We find that PFAS partitioning enhances vesicle diffusiophoresis, consistent with a model combining the Nernst-Planck and Langmuir adsorption equations. Desorption experiments, together with quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring (QCM-D), further reveal that substantial lipid loss occurs during PFAS partitioning. We attribute this loss to lipophobic interactions between the fluorocarbon chains of PFAS and the alkyl chains of lipids. Our findings provide new mechanistic insights into how PFAS may disrupt biological systems.

title: Langmuir kinetics and totally asymmetric volume exclusion in linear chains via Fock space formalism
abstract: Driven-diffusive systems combining spatial exclusion and bulk exchange, such as the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process coupled with Langmuir kinetics (TASEP-LK), serve as foundational models for particle transport in vehicular traffic, conveyor networks, and mesoscopic flow channels. In this work, we employ an exact Doi-Peliti field-theoretic operator formulation in Fock space to evaluate steady-state observables, continuous phase landscapes, and spatial correlations in finite linear chains up to $k = 16$. By introducing a decomposition in terms of biorthonormal eigenvectors for asymmetric non-Hermitian matrices, the stationary state is calculated directly from the kernel of the quasi-Hamiltonian, completely bypassing the computationally prohibitive complexity of full matrix diagonalization and time-dependent matrix exponentiation. Across distinct rate regimes and global parametric scans, our exact discrete calculations demonstrate that finite-size stochastic fluctuations naturally smear out singular domain walls, producing smooth density profiles and continuous phase crossovers. Finite-size scaling illustrates how local profiles systematically steepen toward the sharp domain wall predicted by continuum field theory as $k \to \infty$. Furthermore, two-point correlation analysis reveals that in slow-kinetics regimes, spatial fluctuations generate strong inter-site cumulants, causing standard mean-field approximations to systematically underestimate joint occupancy probabilities by 50\%. These findings emphasize the necessity of analytical methods for modeling mesoscopic transport systems and short traffic corridors where local stochastic fluctuations and spatial correlations dominate the stationary dynamics.

abstract: Experimental observations and computer simulation of formation and structural properties of so far experimentally never seen electrically charged propagating 3D solitons are reported. The propagating solitons appear spontaneously without an external field in a ferroelectric nematic (NF) liquid crystal under rapid cooling from the antiferroelectric (SmZA) phase. abstract: Molecular dynamics predicts molecular motion from atomic forces and trajectory integration. Density functional theory (DFT) provides first-principles forces, but its $O(N^3)$ cost limits simulations to thousands of atoms; empirical force fields scale to millions but miss bond breaking and charge transfer. Equivariant message-passing Transformers learn the ab initio potential at linear cost. Stacked layers propagate information beyond a single cutoff, giving four layers a receptive field up to 23Å. At this frontier, scale is limited by communication: layers exchange boundary features across devices, force backpropagation repeats the exchange, and moving atoms change neighbor graphs and tensor shapes. We present Tessera, a distributed runtime that fixes workload shapes between rebuilds. It sorts atoms along a space-filling curve into equal-count shards, ensuring identical atom counts and tensor shapes per rank. Peer sets scale as $K^{0.5}$, not $K$. A conservative neighbor skin preserves topology across updates, enabling each rebuild interval to replay as one CUDA Graph. Fused kernels, three-level neighbor search, and overlapped All-to-All complete it. On 512 GPUs, Tessera sustains 30.7M atoms at 89.7% weak-scaling efficiency (77--90% across three per-GPU loads); per-step time rises 1.11--1.29x as machine and problem grow 16x. Graph reuse cuts full-step time $1.87\times$. Across an $8\times$ device increase, neighbor-search cost grows $1.7\times$, versus $3.0\times$ for Morton order. In a live $10.24$M-atom salt solution, NVE energy drift is $0.42\,μ$eV/atom/ps over $10$ ps, and structure matches a serial reference. A 10.06M-atom Norovirus capsid sustains 100 ps of NVT at $\approx 8$ ps/day on 256 A100 GPUs. Over 200,000 steps, it has no broken bonds or anomalously close pairs and uses three compiled variants, with no graph breaks or eager fallbacks.

The interface between the malaria parasite
                    Plasmodium spp.
                    and its host erythrocyte critically mediates nutrient uptake, lipid exchange, and protein export required for parasite replication and thus pathogenesis. Approximately half of this interface consists of narrow membrane contact sites, a region defined by only 3 to 4 nm of aqueous space between the parasite plasma membrane and the parasitophorous vacuole membrane. Despite its extent, the region remains largely uncharacterized and inaccessible, not least due to its narrowness. The sole identified resident is the
                    Plasmodium falciparum
                    Niemann-Pick Type C1-Related protein, PfNCR1, an essential Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter, suggesting this conserved transporter family has evolved an unconventional adaptation for localizing to membrane contact sites that can reveal a mechanism to access the region. Here, using live-cell microscopy and assessment of cholesterol homeostasis, we identify a helix–linker–helix (HLH) domain as the necessary modification for efficient PfNCR1 localization. We find that correct localization is required for the parasite to maintain low cholesterol levels, connecting targeting to function. Using a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored fluorescent reporter as a minimal membrane-associated protein, we show that the HLH domain is sufficient to drive localization to the narrow membrane contact site region. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that targeting depends on the physicochemical character of the targeting domain rather than a specific primary sequence, identifying amphipathicity as a determining property of the HLH domain. Taken together, we propose physicochemical partitioning as a fundamental principle for protein targeting at the
                    Plasmodium
                    –erythrocyte interface, and for driving direct functional interactions of a Patched/NPC1-like protein with a second membrane.

abstract: The cytoplasm is a crowded, active medium whose mechanical properties underpin essential cellular functions, yet how intracellular rheology adapts during tissue maturation remains unclear. Here, we examine the evolution of cytoplasmic viscoelasticity in Madin-Darby canine kidney epithelial monolayers as cell density increases. Using magnetic rotational spectroscopy, an active microrheology technique, we quantify zero-shear viscosity and elastic modulus throughout monolayer maturation. We uncover a substantial enhancement of intracellular viscoelasticity correlated with increasing cell density and a concomitant rise in cellular dry mass concentration. Hyperosmotic perturbations on subconfluent monolayers reproduce this effect, confirming cytoplasmic crowding as a driver of rheological changes. Notably, intracellular viscoelasticity scales linearly with dry mass concentration, suggesting a direct coupling between internal mechanics and cytoplasmic concentration during epithelial maturation. These findings establish a link between tissue-level organization and intracellular mechanics, highlighting cytoplasmic crowding as a regulator of epithelial homeostasis and providing a framework to connect rheology with tissue behavior.

title: TRPP Ion Channels Function in the π-Conformation Rather Than the α-Conformation
abstract: PKD2 (TRPP1) is a TRPP ion channel whose dysfunction causes autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Understanding its conformational states and gating mechanism is important for elucidating its function and for structure-based drug discovery. Cryo-EM structures of WT-PKD2 contain a local {pi}-helical turn in the S6 pore-lining helix ({pi}-conformation). In contrast, a fully -helical S6 (-conformation) was observed in the gain-of-function mutant F604P-PKD2 and interpreted as the open state, leading to the proposed {pi}-to- activation mechanism. However, whether the -conformation can support function has never been directly established. Here, using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the functional properties of the -and {pi}-conformations of PKD2. The -conformation remains dewetted unless the lower gate is widened beyond the conformational range observed in mammalian TRP channels. By contrast, the {pi}-conformation supports pore hydration and ion conduction following a small opening of the L677 gate, with simulated conductance comparable to experimental measurements. The closely related PKD2L1 (TRPP2) channel shows a similar dependence on conformation, with a hydrated {pi}-conformation and a dewetted -conformation. Together, these findings challenge the assignment of the -conformation as the conductive state and support a model in which the {pi}-conformation represents the functionally relevant state of TRPP channels. This model suggests that activation may involve an -to-{pi} transition rather than the previously proposed {pi}-to- transition, providing a new framework for understanding TRPP channel gating. This work sheds light on the molecular basis of polycystin channel dysfunction and could facilitate the development of PKD2-targeted therapeutic strategies for ADPKD.

title: The binding landscape of Ras/effector interactions provides insights on Ras switching and oncogenesis
abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) regulate essential cellular processes, yet the evolutionary principles that shape their specificity, adaptability, and dysregulation in disease remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the evolution of a signaling PPI between the small GTPase Ras and its effector Nore1A, a tumor suppressor involved in Ras-mediated signaling. Ras acts as a molecular switch, engaging effectors in its GTP-bound active state and releasing them after GTP hydrolysis, whereas oncogenic mutations such as G12D lock Ras in the active state, promoting aberrant signaling in cancer. Using yeast surface display, deep mutational scanning, and data normalization, we systematically mapped the Ras/Nore1A binding landscape under different physiological and oncogenic states. We generated and screened $\sim$33,000 Nore1A single and double mutants against RasWT and RasG12D in both GTP- and GDP-bound states. Our data revealed that most Nore1A mutations produce small-to-moderate decrease in Ras affinity, while a small number of substitutions enhance affinity. Unexpectedly, GTP hydrolysis causes minimal remodeling of the interaction landscape. Conversely, the oncogenic RasG12D mutation reshapes the binding landscape, revealing many Nore1A variants with enhanced and selective affinity for mutant Ras. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of Nore1A-Ras variant complexes suggest that the non-optimality of the Nore1A/RasG12D binding landscape arises, in part, from the greater intrinsic flexibility of RasG12D and the pronounced reduction in flexibility induced by affinity-enhancing Nore1A mutations. These findings demonstrate that disease-associated mutations can create new evolutionary trajectories in signaling PPIs by changing interaction dynamics and provide a framework for engineering selective protein-based inhibitors targeting oncogenic Ras variants.

abstract: The RNA-binding protein Hfq and inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) were previously suggested to promote DNA compaction of AT-rich regions by forming heterochromatin-like structures, yet the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. Here, we combine coarse-grained and all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the interplay between Hfq, polyP, and DNA. Under physiological conditions, polyP electrostatically interacts with the distal faces of multiple Hfq hexamers, clustering them near DNA and leaving the proximal faces available to interact with the DNA minor groove via the disordered N-termini, thereby promoting compaction.

title: Growth-driven mechanical buckling as a mechanism of age-related tortuosity in human cerebral arteries
abstract: Human cerebral arteries become increasingly, sometimes abnormally, winding with age, but the mechanical basis of this change remains incompletely understood. To examine how arterial bends form and what sets their spacing, we modeled a cerebral artery as a slender elastic vessel supported by surrounding tissue. The distance between its ends remains constant, and the vessel can bend only in a plane tangent to the brain surface. As its natural length increases, axial compression builds until the vessel buckles. Bending partly relieves the compression, and the resulting waves grow in amplitude as elongation continues. Arterial bending stiffness and tissue support determine the wavelength, which is much larger than and proportional to vessel diameter, with comparatively weak dependence on other parameters. Numerical simulations captured a pre-buckling phase, rapid amplification of waves, and slow post-buckling growth during continued elongation. We evaluated these predictions using three-dimensional centerlines of cerebral arteries reconstructed from magnetic resonance angiography in healthy adults. Older age was associated with greater arterial length and excess-length ratio. For arterial waves oriented mostly parallel to the brain surface, wavelength increased with vessel diameter. Both this relationship and the observed wavelength-to-diameter ratio were consistent with model predictions. However, wave amplitude was not significantly associated with age. Overall, the modeling and imaging results support growth-driven buckling and post-buckling deformation under spatial constraint as a plausible mechanical explanation for age-related cerebral arterial tortuosity. This framework links vascular aging to growth-driven instability and pattern formation, with potential applications to diseased arteries beyond the brain.

title: Amyloid stability and condensate material properties independently govern the hnRNPA2 condensate to fibril transition
abstract: hnRNPA2 is a component of cellular membraneless organelles many of which contain RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). RBPs frequently contain low-complexity domains (LCDs) that can also assemble into amyloid fibrils. Fibrils isolated from patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration contain ordered segments of these LCDs and disease-associated mutations can enhance the homotypic interactions that promote aggregation. Although previous studies have largely examined the condensate-to-fibril transition by altering condensate stability, how amyloid structure governs this process remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the hnRNPA2 LCD forms a reproducible fibril fold and by combining structure-guided thermodynamic profiling, peptide design, mutagenesis and in vitro characterization under conditions with (two-phase) and without (one-phase) condensates, we define the molecular determinants of its assembly. We identify an aromatic triad within the fibril core that controls fibril formation kinetics and thermodynamic stability. Mutational analysis further reveals that condensate stability and fibril stability are largely independent. Finally, microrheology linked reduced condensate viscosity to faster fibril formation, supporting a role for condensate material properties in regulating aggregation kinetics. Together, these findings support a model in which the condensate-to-fibril transition is governed by the interplay between a disordered ''fuzzy coat'' and a fibril-forming aromatic triad within hnRNPA2. This work provides a structural framework for understanding how condensates can transition into amyloid assemblies.

title: Lipidic α-synuclein fibrils catalyze the formation of pathological mature fibrils
abstract: The aggregation of -synuclein into amyloid fibrils is a hallmark of a collection of neurodegenerative diseases termed synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease (PD). Interactions between -synuclein and lipid membranes modulate -synuclein aggregation and can produce protofibril structures consisting of both protein and lipid, termed lipidic fibrils. These lipidic fibrils can mature into mature fibrils, which resemble ex vivo fibrils extracted from Lewy bodies found in post-mortem brain samples of PD patients. Here, through the combination of experiments and kinetic theory, we study the influence of lipids and lipidic fibrils on the formation of mature fibrils. We find that lipidic fibrils catalyze mature fibril formation via a heterogeneous primary nucleation mechanism, which lowers the activation energy barrier of mature fibril formation relative to lipid-independent primary nucleation. The final stage of the reaction is governed by mature fibril elongation becoming limited by the rate at which protein monomers dissociate from the metastable lipidic fibrils, confirming that fibrils form in order of stability following Ostwald's Rule of Stages. This mechanism is validated using the small molecule inhibitor ambroxol, which selectively suppresses the formation of lipidic fibrils and in this manner shifts the aggregation kinetics to the slow, lipid-independent pathway. Taken together, these findings reveal that lipidic fibrils act as on-pathway intermediates and accelerate the aggregation of mature fibrils, which could provide a quantitative framework to design novel therapeutic strategies to inhibit pathological -synuclein aggregation.

title: Medial Model of Elastic Curve Contacts, from Clasps to Knits
abstract: Materials constructed from interlocking and tangled fibers are challenging to model and understand due in part to the complex interplay between fiber shape and contact mechanics. Much of our intuition about contact mechanics comes from the Hertzian description, which is based on interactions between convex bodies. However, fibers often form clasp shapes, which involve saddle-shaped contact surfaces; the ability for two interacting bodies to conform to each other along a saddle surface confounds many existing mechanical contact models. Following an observation that contact surfaces between fibers tend to look like minimal, constant mean-curvature surfaces, we seek to test this hypothesis and provide a direct link to geometric modeling methods. To do this, we leverage the medial axis transformation, which generalizes the notion of a Voronoi tessellation to generating curves and surfaces. Through computational studies on an orthogonal clasp and a simple knit structure, we find that the medial axis transformation provides a reasonable model for contact surfaces between identical curves. We also show that a generalization of the medial axis transformation based on radical Voronoi tessellations can be used to well-approximate contact surfaces between non-identical curves. We apply this ``radical axis transform'' to curves of different radii and demonstrate a trend for surfaces to adopt finite mean curvature. Our results may point the way towards more sophisticated geometric methods for modeling tangles.

title: How symmetry and complexity shape three-dimensional programmable self-assembly
abstract: Self-assembly enables complex structures to emerge from simple building blocks through local interaction rules. Are some structures intrinsically easier to design, that is, do they admit more sets of assembly rules than others? And, can this be predicted from their geometry? We address these questions using a three-dimensional polycube model with programmable face-to-face binding, defining a structure's assembly rule probability as the chance that a randomly chosen rule set produces it. For polycubes, this probability decreases exponentially with assembly complexity, the minimum information required to specify a structure's assembly rules. Intuitively, this follows because structures with low assembly complexity are generated not only by minimal rule sets but also by numerous more elaborate ones, and so arise disproportionately often. Symmetry can reduce assembly complexity by allowing the same building blocks and local interactions to be reused across different parts of a structure. Indeed, we find that the highest probability structures come from a tiny subset of highly symmetric structures. However, symmetry alone does not determine assembly complexity. Structures with the same symmetry can differ substantially in the amount of assembly information they require, depending on how effectively their global symmetry can be exploited by local growth rules. Overall, our results link information, symmetry, and assembly rule probability and suggest that identifying which geometric features permit rule reuse is central to designing minimal programmable self-assembling systems.

title: Exploring the World of Lipids with Machine-Learned Coarse-Grained Models
abstract: Lipid bilayers are central to cellular organization and function, yet their atomistic modelling remains constrained by its high computational cost. While coarse-grained (CG) models can overcome this bottleneck, they are limited in accuracy due to the use of simplified functional forms based on molecular mechanics. Using a hybrid functional form combining physics-based terms with a graph neural network, we present implicit-solvent, machine-learned CG models for POPC. When trained on single-lipid data, the model recovers the atomistic conformational landscape. By adding short atomistic simulations of a small flat bilayer to the training data and combining force matching with a denoising objective, we train a model that accurately reproduces bilayer structure and dynamics, in closer agreement with the atomistic reference than existing models, like Martini3 and DryMartini. Beyond its training data, the model stabilizes curved geometries, including vesicles, and captures complex cooperative phenomena such as bilayer and vesicle self-assembly and pore sealing. While limitations remain, particularly regarding chemical transferability, our results establish machine-learned coarse-grained potentials as a promising path towards robust and accurate CG models of lipids and membranes.

title: Designing tunable hyperuniformity in random organization through nonlocal noise
abstract: Hyperuniform fluids suppress density fluctuations at large length scales, but microscopic protocols for designing their asymptotic scaling remain limited. Here we show how effective driving noise generated by particle dynamics can select the hyperuniform exponent while preserving ordinary diffusion and pairwise center-of-mass conservation of the organized particles. We establish this connection through two protocols based on biased random organization (BRO). First, a two-dimensional BRO layer is nonreciprocally coupled to a three-dimensional Brownian gas through density-dependent kick amplitudes. Bulk density fluctuations generate spatially nonlocal noise with a $q^3$ power spectrum in the adiabatic limit, producing $S(q\to0)\sim q^1$. Second, we introduce reciprocal kicks whose lengths follow a Pareto-like distribution, $P(\ell)\sim\ell^{-1-b}$. For $2<b<4$, the finite second moment supports ordinary diffusion, while the divergent fourth moment changes the long-wavelength noise spectrum to $q^b$. The corresponding fluctuating density field theory predicts continuously tunable hyperuniform scaling, $S(q\to0)\sim q^{b-2}$, supported by particle simulations. Together, these results connect targeted hyperuniform scaling to explicit microscopic dynamics and provide a physical basis for designing collective density correlations in nonequilibrium particle systems.

title: Long-time Brownian dynamics of hard and sticky colloids by geometric projection
abstract: Particle-resolved colloid simulations are often limited by the fastest microscopic time scale retained in the model, which can be many orders of magnitude shorter than the collective process of interest. This is especially restrictive for aggregating colloids, where explicit near-contact potentials force the time integration to resolve the rapid positional relaxation of bonded pairs within narrow attractive wells. Here we introduce an overdamped constraint-based Brownian dynamics method that replaces the time-resolved integration of stiff near-contact forces by a geometric projection step. After each free Brownian update, hard-sphere exclusion, sticky bonds, and hard-wall interactions are enforced by projecting the particle positions onto the constrained configuration set. The method preserves hard-sphere structure and diffusion, recovers the aggregation kinetics of sticky hard spheres, and extends the physical time reached at fixed computational cost by one to two orders of magnitude relative to the explicit-potential simulations tested here. This acceleration makes Brownian-dominated, low-Péclet electrophoretic deposition accessible to particle-scale simulations, revealing a pathway in which the suspension first densifies and only subsequently develops a bonded network. Implemented as a LAMMPS fix, the framework provides a modular route to long-time Brownian simulations of dense constrained colloidal systems.

title: Hydrated porous substrates modulate the spatiotemporal dynamics of bacterial turbulence
abstract: Boundary conditions strongly influence bacterial turbulence, motivating the question of how hydrated porous substrates affect near-interface collective motion. We characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of dilute and dense Escherichia coli suspensions above agar substrates of varying concentrations, with glass serving as a nonporous reference. In dense suspensions shortly after loading, collective in-plane kinetic energy varies nonmonotonically with agar concentration, while individual swimming energy and characteristic spatial scales show comparatively little variation. Over five minutes above agar, the collective flow attenuates strongly, accompanied by shorter spatial correlations, longer temporal correlations, and a greater relative spectral weight at higher wavenumbers. To explore how the porous boundary may contribute to these changes, we extend mean-field kinetic theory (MFKT) to incorporate normal seepage and tangential slip at the interface. Linear stability analysis distinguishes near-interface collective modes from those in the bulk and identifies how fluid-layer thickness and permeability-dependent slip length modify the instability cutoff. The predicted reduction in the associated length scale provides a qualitative interpretation of the smaller flow structures observed over time and at higher agar concentrations. These findings reveal distinct substrate-dependent changes in the intensity, persistence, and spatial organization of near-interface bacterial turbulence.
